title: Candles in Leipzig (1989)
hookLine: Monday prayers for peace in St. Nicholas Church become peaceful marches with candles, and soon the Wall is open

lines: OUT INTO THE DARK, WITH CANDLES.
cards: Monday evening in the East German city of Leipzig. Outside St. Nicholas Church, a sign says the church is open to all.

Inside, the pews fill. Some people come every week to pray for peace. Some haven't been inside a church in their lives, and come because it's one of the few rooms in town where people say out loud what they think.
A pastor reads, people pray, someone speaks about the country. Then the doors open, the crowd steps out into the dark square, and many of them are holding lit candles.

teach.b: East Germany was a communist state that watched its people closely. The churches were tolerated, barely, and became a kind of shelter for honest talk. In Leipzig, St.

Nicholas held prayers for peace every Monday, and its pastor, Christian Führer, kept the doors open to anyone: believers, doubters, people who wanted to leave the country, people who wanted to change it.
Church peace groups wore a badge of a man beating a sword into a plow, a line found in the prophets Isaiah and Micah.
In the King James Bible: "they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks." Then the prayers spilled into the streets.

After the service, people walked the ring road around the city center, more of them as the weeks went on, holding candles and calling out: no violence, and, we are the people. Here's the detail people in Leipzig tell.

teach.h: ONE HAND FOR THE CANDLE, ONE TO SHIELD.
teach.b: If you carry a candle in the open air, you need one hand to hold it and the other to shield the flame. That leaves no hand free for a stone.
On one Monday that autumn, soldiers and police were ready, and people feared shooting. It didn't come. Not long after, the Berlin Wall opened.
A remark often credited to an East German leader puts it plainly: they were prepared for everything, except candles and prayers.
Historians name other causes for the fall: the economy, Moscow's changes, a border opening elsewhere. The prayers weren't the whole story.
But they were in it, and so were Jesus's words: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God."

how: St. Nicholas Church in Leipzig still holds Monday prayers for peace. In churches of several traditions, Christians light candles as a sign of prayer, including prayer for peace.

games.why: the crowd walked with candles, calling out no violence. the shooting people feared didn't come.

practice: If you can light a candle safely, do; if not, a lamp or a phone's light will do. Cup your hands around it, the way they did in Leipzig, and notice that your hands are full.
Then hold one place, near or far, where people need peace tonight, and if you pray, pray for it.

wordCard.voice: Peacemakers. Leipzig's Monday prayers for peace that became candlelit marches with no violence, part of how the wall came down.

carryVoice: Your line: candles and prayers. Hands too full to hold a stone. See you tomorrow.
